summary: A landowner pays the last hired the same as the first, then asks whether his goodness gives anyone cause for an evil eye.

context.title: Labourers in the vineyard
paragraphs: Only Matthew tells this parable. [c1] He places it straight after Peter asks what the disciples will receive for leaving everything, so its first hearers are the disciples. [c2] The saying about the last and the first closes chapter 19 and closes the parable too, framing it on both sides. [c3]

A vineyard was a familiar picture of Israel, most clearly in Isaiah’s song of the vineyard. [c4] One long line of interpreters has read the first hired as Israel and the latecomers as the Gentiles. [c5]

The workers are day-labourers waiting in the market-place for hire: free men, but lower in security than the household slaves. [c6] The day was counted in twelve hours from sunrise, so the third hour is mid-morning and the eleventh is late afternoon. [c7] Those hired at the eleventh hour had about one hour of work left. [c8]

The agreed pay, a denarius, was a Roman silver coin and the usual wage for a day’s work. [c9] It was a fair and adequate wage rather than a lavish one. [c10] Paying everyone at evening keeps the Mosaic rule that a day-labourer’s wage is not held back overnight. [c11]

translationNotes.summary: Greek asks “is your eye evil?”, a Jewish idiom for begrudging another’s good.
translationNotes.body: An evil eye was the Hebrew Bible’s image for stinginess and grudging, as in Deut 15:9 and Prov 28:22. [c12] Jewish writings set it against the good eye of the generous giver. [c13] English trades the image for an abstract feeling and loses the echo of Mt 6:22-23, where the same Greek phrase appears. [c14]

translationNotes.summary: The landowner calls himself agathos, the ordinary Greek word for “good”, not a word for generosity as such.
translationNotes.body: Agathos is the everyday word for good. [c15] Lexicons do allow the narrower sense kind or generous in this verse. [c16] But a few verses earlier, in Mt 19:17, Jesus uses the same word when he says that only one is good. [c17] Here goodness means giving more than justice requires, so the parable is about who the owner is, not only what he pays. [c18]

translationNotes.summary: Greek names the coin: a denarius, the Roman silver piece usually paid for a day’s labour.
translationNotes.body: The Greek names a denarius, a Latin loanword for a Roman silver coin, which was the usual pay for a day’s work. [c9] A daily wage is the right sense, but the coin also anchors the later scene in which each worker receives the same piece. [c19]

translationNotes.summary: Hetaire means “comrade”: a cool, even reproving form of address, not a term of affection.
translationNotes.body: Hetairos means comrade or companion and does not imply affectionate friendship. [c20] Matthew puts the same address on Jesus’ lips for the guest without a wedding garment and for Judas, each time with a note of reproof. [c21]

claims.text: The parable of the labourers in the vineyard is recorded only in Matthew.
The parable is spoken in response to Peter’s question in Mt 19:27 about what the disciples will receive.
The saying that the last will be first appears both at Mt 19:30 and at Mt 20:16.
In Isaiah 5:7 the vineyard of the Lord is the house of Israel, and commentators read the vineyard of Mt 20:1 against that background.
A traditional reading, found for example in Matthew Henry, takes the parable as the admission of the Gentiles to equal privileges with the Jews.
The labourers hired in the market-place were free day-labourers, a form of labour lower than that of household slaves.
The Jewish day from sunrise to sunset was divided into twelve hours, so the third hour was about nine in the morning.
The eleventh hour was about five in the afternoon, with about one working hour of the day left.
The denarius (Greek δηνάριον, a Latin loanword) was a Roman silver coin and the usual wage for a day’s work.
A denarius for a day’s work was an adequate and just payment.
The Mosaic law required a hired labourer to be paid on the day of his work (Deut 24:15), and the owner pays at evening.
In the Hebrew Bible an evil eye denotes stinginess, envy or grudging, as in Deut 15:9 and Prov 28:22.
Jewish writings frequently oppose the evil eye to the good eye, which signifies generosity.
Mt 6:23 uses the same Greek phrase, ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός, contrasting the evil eye with the sound eye of Mt 6:22.
The general sense of ἀγαθός is good, excellent in any respect.
Thayer’s lexicon lists Mt 20:15 under the narrower sense of ἀγαθός: benevolent, kind, generous.
In Mt 19:17 Jesus says that only one is good, using ἀγαθός.
In Mt 20:15 the one who is good is the one who gives more than justice requires.
In Mt 20:9-10 each worker, first and last alike, receives a denarius.
Ἑταῖρος means comrade or companion, used of a temporary connection without the idea of affectionate friendship.
Matthew uses the address ἑταῖρε also in Mt 22:12 (the guest without a wedding garment) and Mt 26:50 (Judas), in a tone of reproof.
